extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, academic researchers, and research policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Critically assess the design, incentives, processes, and future options for the scholarly peer-review system, with attention to practical, ethical, and institutional implications. The page is an opinion piece offering reflections and proposed alternatives (AI-based review; institutional/funder endorsement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer availability / reviewer fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: The publishing industry is currently publishing an unreal amount of research which demands millions of peer reviewers. There is an increasing level of inertia among potential peer reviewers across the community; more researchers declining review invitations, even authors who have recently published articles in the host journal, indicates that peer review is no longer seen as a 'good karma' activity by many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge whether a peer-review system is sustainable given reviewer supply. Indicators include volume of submissions per reviewer, rate of invitation declines, time spent recruiting reviewers, and whether delays are driven by recruiting reviewers versus reviewers returning reports. Systems should minimize reliance on scarce volunteer labor or provide mechanisms to expand reviewer capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and delays caused by reviewer recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: The painful delays in the peer-review process have long been recognized. These delays are caused less and less by reviewers being slow in returning their reports, and more and more by the amount of time wasted to getting reviewers to agree to review a manuscript in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate workflows by separating time-to-decision into (a) time to recruit reviewers and (b) time reviewers take to complete reviews. A strong system reduces recruitment delays (e.g., better incentives, alternative review models, or automation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does peer review foster collaboration or merely enforce compliance?
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is now a compliance issue. It doesn’t nurture a culture of collaboration. The peer-review process is seen as a part of compliance. We do authors and reviewers a disservice when we forget that the goal of what should be a collaborative process is to improve the paper and to collectively take the discipline forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge systems by whether they encourage constructive, collaborative interactions (authors and reviewers working to improve work) versus bureaucratic tick-box or policing behaviors. Watch for practices that treat review as mere compliance (e.g., repetitive 'compliance checks' that add little value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity across review rounds and editorial responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When the first-round reviewers decline to review a revised manuscript, often a new set of reviewers is invited in. Those new reviewers are checking the manuscript for the first time, and so new comments and requests are introduced beyond those of the first round of review. If the new second-round reviewers are only being asked to ensure the authors have responded to the first round of review comments, isn’t this something that the editor could do themselves?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether editorial workflows preserve continuity between rounds (same reviewers where appropriate) and whether editors are empowered to judge responses rather than routinely re-starting review cycles. Good practice: editors take responsibility for assessing whether authors have adequately addressed prior comments, avoiding unnecessary reviewer turnover that introduces new, late-stage demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity and role consistency between reviewers and authors
rubrics_metrics.description: All peer reviewers are also authors of journal articles... There is often a disconnect for researchers when serving in these separate roles, creating a contradiction where they feel free to make outrageous demands when reviewing, yet react angrily when the same thing happens to them as authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a normative criterion: reviewers should apply the same standards and empathy they expect when they are authors. Training, codes of conduct, or documented expectations can reduce double standards and encourage fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer incentives, rewards, and conflict-of-interest risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers remain the only entity involved in publishing workflow who receive zero financial incentives for their services, in almost all journals. Monetizing the journal-reviewer relationship has been widely criticized, since some kind of reward system might challenge the motivational aspect of peer review. One reason is, it will significantly increase journal publication costs to develop and run a reviewer payment system. But more importantly, such a payment will cause a conflict of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether and how a system compensates reviewers, balancing fair recognition (payments, badges, certificates, public acknowledgement) against risks of creating conflicts of interest or escalating costs. Consider alternatives (institutional recognition, FTE credit) and the downstream financial impacts (APCs, library costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for authors’ research journey and appropriateness of reviewer judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A research manuscript is an output coming at the end of a fairly long process... But, can we truly justify why a couple of subject matter specialists—who have no knowledge of the deep, personal journey of the researchers—are qualified to judge the latter’s manuscript and to recommend if it is worthy of sharing with the world or not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to examine whether review practices fairly acknowledge the broader research process and the collective work of teams/institutions. Consider whether reviews focus solely on narrow technical points or also consider the context, effort, and intent behind the work. Beware of processes that reduce complex projects to the judgement of a few detached specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer accountability and transparency when things go wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers have responsibilities, but are not responsible for any dark side of publishing. When a journal article gets retracted or even removed, we see how authors, editors, and publishers get blamed for not performing their duties... But, despite their ‘guardianship’, have we ever seen a peer reviewer be named and shamed for being part of a retraction shambles and blacklisted? Persecuted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the system has appropriate mechanisms for accountability, for learning from reviewer mistakes, and for balancing anonymity with responsibility. Consider how open review affects the ability to identify and remediate reviewer errors and whether there are proportionate consequences or corrective processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of peer review in career advancement and institutional incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is a researcher’s scholarly contribution that is not appreciated in almost all academic/research institutions’ career advancement qualifications (or funders’ decisions for where to award grants). And publishers are doing nothing to change administrators’ mindset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge systems by whether they embed peer review in evaluation and reward structures (promotion, tenure, funding). Strong systems credit and count peer-review service (e.g., documented hours, recognised contributions) so that reviewers are not purely volunteering invisible labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative value of peer review vs. non-peer-reviewed outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: In a world, where non-peer-reviewed research documents (including pre-prints) are getting endorsed by being cited in peer-reviewed journal articles and seen as entirely sufficient by some funding agencies, what is the value of peer review?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to evaluate the functional value of peer review in the current ecosystem: if other mechanisms (preprints, funder checks, citations) serve the same social/legal/policy functions, question whether traditional pre-publication peer review is providing unique value warranting its costs and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility and acceptability of GenAI-based article review
rubrics_metrics.description: Our publishing future will inevitably be shaped by GenAI. Peer reviewers are already using GenAI tools to review papers. I imagine, and advocate for, a rapid improvement of the existing and budding elements of a GenAI-based article review system. Given the current pace, we may see some pioneering journals moved to a 100% GenAI-based review system by 2026, if not earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess AI-driven review systems on accuracy, bias, transparency, explainability, and community acceptance. Criteria include whether AI can reliably check methodology and integrity, how humans are kept in the loop, potential failure modes, and whether stakeholders accept AI judgments as legitimate substitutes for human appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional or funder-led internal review and endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Take away review responsibility from publishers and give it to the host institutions and research funders. Respective institutional research review committees (RRCs) will be responsible for internally reviewing research manuscripts produced by their research staff, and ensuring its quality. A final manuscript will then be submitted to a journal along with an endorsement letter signed by the head of the institution... The journal, if finding the manuscript matching its scope, will do light editing and formatting, communicate minor questions or clarifications to the corresponding author, finalize the piece, and publish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a proposed structural alternative: evaluate institutional capacity, incentives (institutional reputation at stake), processes for multi-institutional work (lead institution endorses), and parallels to other institutional committees (ethics, procurement). Consider safeguards against bias, rubber-stamping, and unequal capacities across institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity and capacity of institutions to perform review
rubrics_metrics.description: This arrangement should enhance both research and publishing integrity... This arrangement (i.e., internal review then institutional endorsement) can raise the issue of biasness. I would argue that if we believe all other institutional committees... are honestly performing their duties, why it can’t be the same done for research papers? (Commenters challenge this: who pays, who has expertise, unequal resources, small institutions and independent researchers excluded.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure any institutional-review proposal against equity: whether smaller or less-funded institutions (and unaffiliated/independent researchers) would be excluded, whether institutions have the disciplinary expertise to review internally, and who would fund the necessary infrastructure and staff time. Include contingency plans for researchers outside well-resourced institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal neutrality, editorial gatekeeping, and the role of publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a reason why journals exist, and that’s largely to provide a neutral, third party review of research results and claims. Allowing researchers (or their employers) to review their own work removes that neutrality from the situation... If the journal exists to simply rubber stamp their approval, then why have a journal at all? Why would anyone need Nature if it's just a collection of stuff already approved by universities and no judgements are made on it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether proposals preserve journals' role as neutral arbiters that provide credibility and trust to the literature. Consider how institutional or funder review would affect journals' unique functions (scope selection, impartial assessment) and whether journals would retain added value beyond formatting and editing.
